The test image shows a close-up of a red/orange tomato fruit surface covered with multiple dark, spiky/bristly circular fungal structures (acervuli with setae) and some white mycelium in the center. This pattern is characteristic of Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.).

Let me view reference images across 8 different classes to confirm.

Based on my analysis:

**Test image key features:**
- Red/orange tomato fruit surface (close-up macro view)
- Multiple dark circular structures with radiating spines/bristles (setae)
- White mycelium clustered in center
- Bugwood ID 5475192 (sequential to Anthracnose reference 5475194 — same photographer/submission)

**Reference comparison:**
- Anthracnose references confirmed tomato fruit involvement with dark acervuli; the spiky/bristly radiating structures are characteristic Colletotrichum acervuli with setae
- Alternaria references showed stem cankers and microscopic conidia — no fruit surface match
- Gray Mold showed fuzzy gray growth, not spiky dark structures
- Rhizopus showed round sporangia on hyphae without radiating setae
- Septoria was on leaves with simple round spots

The dark sea-urchin-like structures with radiating bristles on the red tomato fruit surface are the defining visual signature of Colletotrichum acervuli with setae, and the sequential Bugwood IDs confirm this is from the same Anthracnose image set.
